paragraphs: Educated in the enervating way recommended by the writers I have been criticizing, and with no chance, given their subordinate position in society, of recovering their lost ground, is it surprising that women everywhere appear to be a defect in nature? Is it surprising, when we consider how decisive an effect an early association of ideas has on the character, that they neglect their understandings and turn all their attention to their persons?

The great advantages that naturally follow from stocking the mind with knowledge are obvious from the following considerations. The association of our ideas is either habitual or instantaneous, and the latter kind seems to depend on the original temperament of the mind rather than on the will. Once ideas and matters of fact have been taken in, they lie in reserve until some chance circumstance makes information received at very different periods of our lives dart into the mind with illuminating force. Many recollections are like a flash of lightning, one idea assimilating and explaining another with astonishing speed. I am not now referring to that quick perception of truth which is so intuitive that it defies investigation, and leaves us at a loss to decide whether it is memory or reasoning, lost to sight in its swiftness, that opens the dark cloud. Over those instantaneous associations we have little power; for once the mind has been enlarged by wide-ranging flights or deep reflection, the raw materials will, to some degree, arrange themselves of their own accord. The understanding, it is true, may keep us from drawing out of proportion when we group our thoughts, or when we copy the warm sketches of fancy from the imagination; but the animal spirits, the individual character, supply the colouring. Over this subtle electric fluid,* how little power we have, and how little power reason can gain over it! These fine, intractable spirits seem to be the essence of genius, and, beaming in its eagle eye, they produce in the highest degree that happy energy of associating thoughts which surprises, delights and instructs. These are the glowing minds that concentrate pictures for their fellow creatures, forcing them to view with interest objects, reflected from the impassioned imagination, which they had passed over in nature.

(*Footnote. I have sometimes, when inclined to laugh at materialists, asked whether, since the most powerful effects in nature are apparently produced by fluids — the magnetic, etc. — the passions might not be fine volatile fluids that embraced humanity, holding its more refractory elementary parts together — or whether they were simply a liquid fire that pervaded the more sluggish materials, giving them life and heat?)

I must be allowed to explain myself. Most people cannot see or feel poetically; they lack imagination, and therefore flee from solitude in search of objects for the senses. But when an author lends them his eyes, they can see as he saw, and be entertained by images they could not pick out for themselves, though these lay before them.

Education, then, only supplies the man of genius with knowledge that gives variety and contrast to his associations. But there is a habitual association of ideas, which grows “with our growth,” that has a great effect on the moral character of mankind, and which gives the mind a bent that usually remains throughout life. The understanding is so pliable, and yet so stubborn, that associations formed by chance circumstances during the years in which the body grows to maturity can seldom be disentangled by reason. One idea calls up another, its old associate, and memory, faithful to first impressions, especially when the intellectual powers are not employed to cool our sensations, retraces them with mechanical exactness.

This habitual slavery to first impressions has a more harmful effect on the female character than on the male, because business and other dry employments of the understanding tend to deaden the feelings and to break up associations that do violence to reason. But females, who are made into women while they are still mere children, and brought back to childhood when they ought to have left the baby-walker behind forever, do not have enough strength of mind to wipe away the artificial layers that have smothered nature.

Everything they see or hear serves to fix impressions, call forth emotions and associate ideas that give their minds a sexual character. False notions of beauty and delicacy stunt the growth of their limbs and produce a sickly tenderness rather than delicacy of organs; and, weakened in this way by being occupied in unfolding, instead of examining, the first associations forced on them by everything around them, how can they attain the vigour they need to throw off their artificial character? — where can they find the strength to fall back on reason and rise above a system of oppression that blasts the fair promise of spring? This cruel association of ideas, which everything conspires to twist into all their habits of thinking — or, to speak more precisely, of feeling — gains new force when they begin to act a little for themselves; for they then perceive that it is only through their skill in exciting emotions in men that pleasure and power are to be gained. Besides, all the books expressly written for their instruction, which make the first impression on their minds, instil the same opinions. Since they are educated in worse than Egyptian bondage, it is unreasonable, as well as cruel, to reproach them for faults that can scarcely be avoided, unless we suppose a degree of native vigour that falls to the lot of very few among mankind.

For instance, the harshest sarcasms have been aimed at the sex, and women have been ridiculed for repeating “a set of phrases learnt by rote,” when nothing could be more natural, given the education they receive, and given that their “highest praise is to obey, unargued” — the will of man. If they are not allowed enough reason to govern their own conduct — why, all they learn must be learned by rote! And when all their ingenuity is called upon to arrange their dress, “a passion for a scarlet coat” is so natural that it has never surprised me; and, granting that Pope’s summary of their character is just, “that every woman is at heart a rake,” why should they be bitterly censured for seeking a kindred mind and preferring a rake to a man of sense?

Rakes know how to work on their sensibility, while the modest merit of reasonable men naturally has less effect on their feelings; and such men cannot reach the heart by way of the understanding, because they have few sentiments in common.

It seems a little absurd to expect women to be more reasonable than men in their LIKINGS while still denying them the unrestricted use of reason. When do men FALL IN LOVE with sense? When do they, with all their superior powers and advantages, turn from the person to the mind? How, then, can they expect women, who are taught only to observe behaviour and to acquire manners rather than morals, to despise what they have spent their whole lives labouring to attain? Where are they suddenly to find judgment enough to weigh patiently the good sense of an awkward but virtuous man, when his manners, of which they have been made critical judges, are off-putting, and his conversation cold and dull because it does not consist of pretty repartees or well-turned compliments? To admire or esteem anything for any length of time, we must at least have our curiosity roused by knowing, to some degree, what we admire; for we are unable to estimate the value of qualities and virtues beyond our comprehension. Such respect, when it is felt, may be very sublime, and the confused consciousness of humility may make the dependent creature an interesting object from some points of view; but human love must have coarser ingredients, and the person will very naturally come in for its share — and an ample share it usually has!

Love is, to a great degree, an arbitrary passion, and, like some other stalking mischiefs, it will reign by its own authority without deigning to reason. It can also easily be distinguished from esteem, the foundation of friendship, because it is often excited by fleeting beauties and graces — though, to give energy to the feeling, something more solid must deepen their impression and set the imagination to work, to make the fairest — the first good.

Common passions are excited by common qualities. Men look for beauty and the simper of good-humoured docility; women are captivated by easy manners. A gentlemanly man seldom fails to please them, and their thirsty ears eagerly drink in the insinuating nothings of politeness, while they turn away from the unintelligible sounds of the charmer — reason, charm he never so wisely. In superficial accomplishments the rake certainly has the advantage; and of these women can form an opinion, for this is their own ground. Made gay and giddy by the whole tenor of their lives, they must find the very look of wisdom, or the severe graces of virtue, gloomy; these produce a kind of restraint against which they and love, that playful child, naturally rebel. Without taste, except of the lighter kind — for taste is the offspring of judgment — how can they discover that true beauty and grace must arise from the play of the mind? And how can they be expected to relish in a lover what they themselves do not possess, or possess only very imperfectly? The sympathy that unites hearts and invites confidence is so very faint in them that it cannot catch fire and so rise to passion. No, I repeat it, the love cherished by such minds must have coarser fuel!

The inference is obvious: until women are led to exercise their understandings, they should not be satirized for their attachment to rakes, nor even for being rakes at heart, when this appears to be the inevitable consequence of their education. Those who live to please must find their enjoyments, their happiness, in pleasure! It is a trite but true remark that we never do anything well unless we love it for its own sake.

Supposing, however, for a moment, that in some future turn of time women were to become what I sincerely wish them to be, even love would acquire a more serious dignity and be purified in its own fires; and, with virtue giving true delicacy to their affections, they would turn from a rake in disgust. Reasoning then, as well as feeling — at present the only province of woman — they could easily guard against outward graces, and would quickly learn to despise the sensibility that had been excited and worn stale in the ways of women whose trade was vice, and by the wanton airs of allurement. They would remember that the flame (one must use appropriate expressions) which they wished to kindle had been exhausted by lust, and that the sated appetite, having lost all relish for pure and simple pleasures, could be roused only by the licentious arts of variety. What satisfaction could a woman of delicacy promise herself in a union with such a man, when the very guilelessness of her affection might seem insipid? This is how Dryden describes the situation:
“Where love is duty on the female side, On theirs mere sensual gust, and sought with surly pride.”

But there is one great truth that women have yet to learn, though it matters greatly to them that they act on it. In choosing a husband they should not be led astray by the qualities of a lover — for a husband, even supposing him to be wise and virtuous, cannot long remain a lover.

If women were educated more rationally, and could take a more comprehensive view of things, they would be content to love only once in their lives, and after marriage calmly let passion subside into friendship — into that tender intimacy which is the best refuge from care, yet which is built on such pure, still affections that idle jealousies would not be allowed to disturb the discharge of the sober duties of life, nor to take up thoughts that ought to be employed otherwise. This is a state in which many men live, but few, very few, women. And the difference can easily be accounted for without resorting to a character peculiar to their sex. Men, for whom, we are told, women were made, have occupied women’s thoughts too much; and this association has so entangled love with all their motives of action that — to harp a little on an old string — having been employed solely either in preparing themselves to excite love or in actually putting their lessons into practice, they cannot live without love. But when a sense of duty, or fear of shame, obliges them to restrain this pampered desire to please beyond certain lengths — too far for delicacy, it is true, though far from criminality — they obstinately resolve to love their husbands (I speak of their passion) to the end of the chapter; and then, acting the part which they foolishly demanded of their lovers, they become abject wooers and doting slaves.

Men of wit and fancy are often rakes, and fancy is the food of love. Such men will inspire passion. Half the sex, in its present childish state, would pine for a Lovelace — a man so witty, so graceful and so brave; and can they DESERVE blame for acting on principles so constantly drummed into them? They want a lover and protector — and behold him kneeling before them: bravery prostrate before beauty! In this way love throws the virtues of a husband into the background, and bright hopes or lively emotions banish reflection until the day of reckoning comes; and come it surely will, to turn the sprightly lover into a surly, suspicious tyrant who contemptuously insults the very weakness he fostered. Or, supposing the rake reformed, he cannot quickly shake off old habits. When a man of ability is first carried away by his passions, sentiment and taste are needed to varnish the enormities of vice and give zest to brutal indulgences; but when the gloss of novelty has worn off and pleasure palls on the senses, lasciviousness becomes barefaced, and enjoyment becomes nothing but the desperate effort of weakness fleeing from reflection as from a legion of devils. Oh, virtue, you are not an empty name! All that life can give — you give!

If much comfort cannot be expected from the friendship of a reformed rake of superior abilities, what follows when he lacks sense as well as principles? Truly, misery in its most hideous form. When the habits of weak people have been hardened by time, reform is barely possible, and it actually makes those beings miserable who have not mind enough to be amused by innocent pleasure. Like the tradesman who retires from the bustle of business, they find that nature presents them with nothing but a universal blank, and their restless thoughts prey on their dampened spirits. Their reformation, like his retirement, actually makes them wretched, because it deprives them of all employment by quenching the hopes and fears that set their sluggish minds in motion.

If such is the force of habit, if such is the bondage of folly, how carefully we ought to guard the mind against storing up vicious associations; and we should be equally careful to cultivate the understanding, to save the poor creature from the weak, dependent state of even harmless ignorance. For it is the right use of reason alone that makes us independent of everything — except the unclouded Reason, “Whose service is perfect freedom.”
